voiceover: POV: your aunt opens your wedding invitation on her phone. Here's what your guests see when they tap your invitation link. I'll also tell you who this doesn't work for. You build a digital wedding invitation on a laptop. So you never see what your guests see. With Wedillybird, guests install no app and make no account. A demo for Léa and Adam, a fictional couple. The envelope fills the screen. The seal carries their initials. It opens, and the invitation appears. This opening is called The Seal. There's a skip button, too. Then the page: the couple's names, and a countdown to the big day. Scroll down, and the date and the venue are right there. Here's the part people skip: the wedding RSVP. Three answers: I'll be there, Maybe, or I can't make it. Say yes, and more fields open: plus-ones, up to the number you allow. Dietary needs go in a plain text box, with room for a note. If this is useful, follow. Entry three of Norah's Notebook lands tomorrow evening. Plans change, and a guest can change their answer later. Then Send, and confetti: Thank you, your reply is saved. Here's who it doesn't work for. Seventy-eight percent of American adults sixty-five and older own a smartphone. That's most of them, not all of them. And owning a phone isn't the same as being at ease with links. A personal link needs a phone, and Wedillybird can't change that. So keep a paper card ready, with a phone number to call. Envelope, page, reply. That's the trip we just watched. See a sample invitation: link in bio. I'm Norah, Wedillybird's AI host. Now you know what your aunt sees.

caption:
Digital wedding invitation: what your guests actually see.
A guest's-eye walk through a demo invitation, from the envelope to the saved reply, plus the one kind of guest who still needs paper. Léa and Adam are a fictional couple.
Hosted by Norah, an AI character created by the Wedillybird team.
pinned_comment: A guest's trip: an envelope opens (The Seal), the page shows the couple's names, a countdown, the date and the venue, then the guest answers: I'll be there, Maybe, or I can't make it. A yes opens plus-ones, dietary needs and a note. Keep a paper card and a phone number ready for guests without a smartphone. Norah is AI-generated. Screens shown are real Wedillybird screens (demo data).
comment_bait: Who on your guest list would need the paper card?

sources.fact: 78% of US adults aged 65+ own a smartphone (90% at ages 50-64)
sources.title: Mobile Fact Sheet

sources.fact: Offer a fallback that is not app-based (paper, phone); the barrier is channel and app familiarity rather than phone ownership
sources.title: Mobile Fact Sheet (smartphone ownership by age); fallback advice per r2 T38 myth-vs-truth

sources.fact: If guests may reply another way, print that option (phone or email) on the response card
sources.title: Wedding Email Dos and Don'ts

numbers_used.source: Pew Research Center, Mobile Fact Sheet, published 2025-11-20 (survey of 5,022 US adults, 5 Feb-18 Jun 2025)

needs_proof: S01 capture should show the L&A seal, the opening and, ideally, the skip button (skip button per r3 B1); if it is not visible, the card text carries it.
S03 capture should show names, countdown, date and venue; the countdown only appears after hydration.
S04 capture should show the three answers, the plus-one / dietary / note fields and the 'Thank you, your reply is saved' confetti.
'A guest can change their answer later' comes from rsvp-form-v4 / convex/rsvps.ts (r3 B1); it is not visible in the demo capture.
claims_review.notes: Fictional couple Léa and Adam named and labelled as fictional in the voice-over. No delivery channel, QR code, number of openings, or choice of opening/music/photo is mentioned. The only figure is Pew 78% (T38), spelled out, with the source on a card. Line 22 (owning a phone is not the same as being at ease with links) is Norah's reasoning from T38's myth-vs-truth, not a sourced statistic. The paper card with a phone number is a suggestion built on T35/T38. Wedillybird is named three times (beats 6, 23, 27).
